implementation_notes: The stdlib provides the mute as a context manager: `with contextlib.suppress(OSError):` suppresses the listed exception types raised in the block and resumes with the statement after it, and the documentation is explicit that, as with any mechanism that completely suppresses exceptions, it 'should be used only to cover very specific errors where silently continuing with program execution is known to be the right thing to do'. That makes the hand-written `try/except SpecificError: pass` the fallback form; when the failure should leave a trace, catch the narrow type and log at debug level instead of suppressing it.
code_sketch:
from contextlib import suppress

# documented: the lock file may already be gone; unlinking is best-effort
with suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    stale_lock.unlink()
with suppress(OSError):        # read-only descriptor: nothing buffered
    handle.close()
pitfalls: Listing several exception types in one suppress() widens the mute: each type needs its own justification; when only one is justified, name only that one.

Suppression also hides the failure from a debugger session (no default post-mortem stop), and the bare `except:` form is worse still - it is not the same thing and violates PEP 8's explicit-exception rule.
Suppressing around more than the single call (a whole body, a loop iteration) turns the idiom into the blanket-catch anti-pattern and hides failures of statements nobody analysed.
